newsitem.title: RWANDA: Aid workers quit eastern Zaire town after shelling.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers quit eastern Zaire town after shelling.

text.p: A group of aid workers left the eastern Zairean town of Bukavu by air on Monday because of heavy firing that Rwanda said Zairean troops started by shelling southwestern Rwanda.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it evacuated three of its seven delegates in Bukavu by air to Kenya because of worsening security.
IFRC official Jon Valfells told Reuters in Nairobi by telephone from the organisation's headquarters in Geneva that indiscriminate shelling began late on Sunday.
"Two shells fell in the garden of the Bukavu hotel where most foreign aid workers stay," he said.

Another IFRC official, John Watt, reported firing which appeared to involve 60 mm and 80 mm mortars and said there was also small arms fire from 9 P.M. to 2 A.M. on Monday (1900 to 2400 GMT) with a one-hour lull.
The IFRC, which runs two refugee camps for 70,000 Rwandan Hutus near Bukavu, said it did not know who was responsible.
Unconfirmed reports said other aid agencies were starting to evacuate.
"Firing started at six o'clock in the evening (on Sunday) and continued (after a lull)...until two in the morning," said Rwandan defence ministry spokesman Major Emmanuel Ndahiro.
"It was the Zairean army, and they used anti-aircraft cannon, 75 mm recoiless rifles and 82 mm mortars to attack army positions around Cyangugu and Kamembe. There were no casualties.
"We returned fire at positions around Bukavu," he added.
He said it was unclear why the Zairean army had attacked but added it was an attempt to destabilise the border region.

The firing followed the Zairean government stepping up its campaign against neighbours Rwanda and Burundi and aid agencies by accusing them of promoting or aiding armed Tutsi infiltrators on missions to destabilise its volatile eastern refugee zone.
Zaire government spokesman Oscar Lugendo said on Saturday Rwanda sent Tutsi infiltrators of the Banyamulenge group, most of whom have lived in eastern Zaire for generations.
The government warned aid agencies caring for the estimated 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in camps in eastern Zaire that they would be banned unless they limited themselves to aid work.
Human rights watchdog Amnesty International on Friday accused Zairean troops and officials of atrocities against Banyamulenge civilians in eastern Zaire over the past month.
There are some 400,000 Banyamulenge, all of whom claim to be Zairean.
The transitional Zairean parliament decided in April they should all be expelled from Zaire with Rwandan Hutu refugees.
"The Zaireans are drawing attention to themselves and are trying to make Zaire's problems everybody's problems," said Ndahiro on Monday, adding Zairean troops operated with Rwandan Hutu rebels.
Residents said six shells were fired from the Zairean side and the Rwandan army returned the fire. They said mortar and machinegun fire in the area continued until early on Monday.
Refugees arriving from Zaire at Bugerama in Cyangugu province, Rwanda, told aid workers at the weekend that Zairean troops and Rwandan Hutu militiamen attacked them as they fled.

The workers quoted the newly arrived refugees as saying that some refugees were beaten, stabbed and more than 30 had their arms and legs bound before being thrown into the Rusizi river, which forms the border between both countries, to drown them.
Rwandan authorities accuse Zaire of supporting Rwandan Hutu militiamen who fled to Zaire with refugees after being involved in the 1994 genocide of up to one million people in Rwanda.
